title: Rebuked in court, ICE stops immediate rearrest tactics in Colorado
text:
Rebuked in court, ICE stops immediate rearrest tactics in Colorado
ICE will no longer immediately rearrest immigrants freed on judges’ orders in Colorado.
After spending more than half a year in an immigration detention center, Emmanuel thought he was free. A federal judge in Colorado had ordered his release, but Immigration and Customs Enforcement had other plans.
“As soon as I stepped outside, there were five ICE officers waiting,” says Emmanuel, who asked to use only that name due to privacy concerns.
The immigrant says he was handcuffed, put in a van, and driven to the back. From there, he was brought back into the Aurora detention center as if he were a new detainee.
ICE has been staging the release of immigrants on judges’ orders, arresting them again, and bringing them back into detention. The tactic is another example of the agency pushing the bounds and stirring skepticism in the judiciary.
“I wasn’t too surprised,” says Emmanuel, who had heard about this tactic. “The whole system is set up to break you.”
A federal judge on Wednesday found an ICE official in civil contempt in a similar redetention case in Colorado. Beginning in late October, ICE’s Denver office subjected at least 18 immigrants to the practice, according to court records. Officers staged a release after a court ordered someone free, followed by redetention within 12 hours.
“Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless,” wrote U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney. She described “unconstitutional behavior that runs top to bottom.”
Immigrant advocates had decried the immediate redetention practice on due process grounds. Before the contempt order against his colleague this week, Nathan Rasper, the acting field office director for ICE in Denver, told the judge he had halted the practice that he believed was legal.
Meanwhile, similar arrests have cropped up elsewhere, at least in Minnesota, and the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, has left the door open for more. The revelations in Colorado come as other federal judges rebuke ICE practices here.
Courts weigh in
After major midterm election losses for Republicans, President Donald Trump said his immigration crackdown might have been “too tough.”
Yet he has also elevated immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. Mr. Miller had previously explored suspending the constitutional right of habeas corpus, which allows people to challenge their detention in court. Immigrants recently rearrested in Colorado had been previously ordered released by federal judges on habeas petitions.
Detention is key to the deportation pipeline. It’s easier for ICE to remove people under its control. Yet as the government claims record-high ICE arrests of more than 50,000 a month, the agency has struggled to keep many in custody due to historic filings of habeas petitions.
Mr. Rasper, who assumed his post in Colorado mid-October, said he’d heard of rearrests from ICE’s office in Minnesota. He saw the practice as lawful if the second arrest was based on fixing the government’s own paperwork errors, such as around issuing what’s called a “notice to appear.” That charging document starts someone’s process in immigration court.
Rearrests were meant to target “public safety concerns,” Mr. Rasper said in a hearing Nov. 9. Given the judge’s concerns, he said he directed the practice to stop and for those rearrested to be released. Through an ICE spokesperson, Mr. Rasper declined an interview.
The American Civil Liberties Union of Colorado, which appeared as a friend of the court, rejected Mr. Rasper’s arguments as lawful grounds for rearrest.
What ICE described as a technical violation is a “fundamental violation of law,” said Tim Macdonald, the group’s legal director. “We’re seeing it repeatedly.”
The judge sided with the immigrant advocates.
“It is a due process violation,” said Judge Sweeney. “ICE is not in a position to monitor its own conduct in terms of legality.”
A week after his release from redetention, another man recounts how officers drove him from the ICE detention center in Aurora to another ICE office nearby, then back to Aurora.
“Very confused. I was scared,” says the man, who requested not to publish his name due to fear of retribution. He recalls a fellow detainee asking ICE officers why they were doing this, and one responding: “We just want to try something.”
The White House referred the Monitor to the DHS.
Break from tradition
Asked by the Monitor if the redetention directive came from Washington, and where else officers have been ordered to follow it, the DHS sent an unsigned statement that didn’t directly address those points. “ICE complies with all lawful court orders,” the email said.
“When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement,” the statement said. “Instead, if ICE does not appeal the ruling, it may seek to re-arrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision.”
Three former ICE attorneys, whose combined careers spanned more than three decades at the agency, told the Monitor they question the legality of the tactic.
To rearrest someone, such as someone released on bond by an immigration judge, there need to be “changed circumstances,” such as new criminal activity on the part of the person released, says Paul Hunker, former longtime chief counsel for ICE in Dallas. “They can’t just arrest the person for no good reason.”
ICE is taking a “maximalist approach,” says Ryan Schwank, an assistant chief counsel at ICE who resigned in February, as a whistleblower on officer training. “They really do interpret things in the way that’s most favorable to themselves. And that’s not good-faith behavior.”
Kerry Doyle, general counsel for ICE under the Biden administration, also says she’s “dubious” of immediate rearrests without a change in circumstances.
Even if the government had a “creative argument,” says Ms. Doyle, the policy adds to the “ongoing undermining of the judiciary ... and the relationship between the federal government and these judges.”
In a separate case before a federal appellate court, the government is appealing a preliminary injunction meant to ensure ICE’s warrantless arrests are lawful, an order that a district judge said ICE defied.
Emmanuel’s immigration case, meanwhile, continues.
He legally entered the United States over two decades ago. But his status expired, and an immigration judge ordered him deported at a hearing that Emmanuel says he didn’t know he needed to attend. As he adjusts back to life with his family, for now, he says he still fears arrest.
In detention, he recalls, an officer asked if he hated this country now.
No, Emmanuel said. His American children were born here.
“If I love my children, I cannot hate where they’re from.”
